title: FlashRAG: a Python toolkit for reproducing and developing RAG research
text: FlashRAG is an open-source Python toolkit for reproducing, comparing and developing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods. The repository is hosted by the RUC-NLPIR group, and its accompanying paper lists authors from the Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence at Renmin University of China (RUC). The toolkit ships implementations of many published RAG algorithms, including reasoning-based methods that combine reasoning with retrieval, together with a large collection of pre-processed benchmark RAG datasets. It provides modular RAG components such as retrievers, generators and refiners; bi-encoder retrievers like DPR, BGE and E5 use Faiss for search, and generators include Fusion-in-Decoder models. RAG methods are grouped into pipeline types according to their inference path. The project also offers a web UI for configuring and trying the baselines, supports multimodal RAG with models such as LLaVA, Qwen and InternVL, and is released under the MIT License.

title: Microsoft GraphRAG: knowledge-graph-based retrieval-augmented generation
text: GraphRAG is a structured, hierarchical approach to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) from Microsoft Research, with its code published in the microsoft/graphrag GitHub repository under the MIT license. Its indexing pipeline uses large language models to pull entities, relationships and key claims out of unstructured text and builds a knowledge graph from them. The graph is clustered hierarchically with the Leiden technique into communities, and summaries of each community are generated from the bottom up. At query time GraphRAG offers several modes: global search answers holistic questions about the whole corpus by using the community summaries; local search reasons about specific entities by fanning out to their neighbors and related concepts; DRIFT search follows the same entity-centered approach with added community context; and basic search falls back to standard top-k vector search. The project warns that indexing can be expensive and strongly recommends tuning its prompts by following the prompt tuning guide.

title: LightRAG: a lightweight knowledge-graph RAG framework from HKU
text: LightRAG is a lightweight knowledge-graph retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework that its authors present as an efficient alternative to Microsoft GraphRAG. It comes from HKUDS, the Data Intelligence Lab at HKU; the accompanying paper lists authors from the University of Hong Kong and Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications. LightRAG brings graph structures into text indexing and retrieval, managing both a knowledge graph and vector embeddings, and uses an incremental update algorithm to add new data. Queries run in several modes: local for specific entities, global for broad themes and cross-document relationships, hybrid combining the two, naive for classic chunk-based retrieval, and mix, the default, which merges local, global and naive results. Storage backends include PostgreSQL, MongoDB, OpenSearch, Milvus, Qdrant, Neo4j and Memgraph. The README also lists reranker support, multimodal processing through RAG-Anything, and RAGAS evaluation with Langfuse tracing. It is MIT licensed.

title: RAGatouille: easy ColBERT late-interaction retrieval for RAG pipelines
text: RAGatouille is a Python library that makes it easy to use and train state-of-the-art retrieval models, chiefly ColBERT, inside any retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. It is hosted under the AnswerDotAI GitHub organization and released under the Apache-2.0 license. With the RAGPretrainedModel class you index a document collection, which is saved to disk, and then search it for the top-k passages for a query. The RAGTrainer class handles training and fine-tuning ColBERT models; its built-in training data processor accepts pairs, labelled pairs and several kinds of triplets, and mines hard negatives by default. The README explains why the late-interaction approach used by ColBERT works well and notes that such models have been shown to generalise better. It lists related integrations: the official ColBERT implementation, Vespa's managed RAG engine with ColBERT support, which is usable from LangChain, Intel's FastRAG, and early ColBERT support in LlamaIndex.

title: ColBERT: reference implementation of late-interaction retrieval (ColBERTv2, PLAID)
text: This repository, hosted under the stanford-futuredata GitHub organization, contains the reference implementation of ColBERT, a fast and accurate retrieval model for scalable BERT-based search over large text collections. ColBERT relies on fine-grained contextual late interaction: it encodes each passage into a matrix of token-level embeddings, encodes each query into another matrix at search time, and finds passages that contextually match the query with scalable vector-similarity MaxSim operators. The stable branch includes ColBERTv2, which brings lightweight late interaction with residual compression, and PLAID, an efficient engine for late-interaction retrieval. The README also lists related papers built on the codebase, such as Baleen for multi-hop reasoning with condensed retrieval and UDAPDR for unsupervised domain adaptation through LLM prompting and distillation of rerankers. It points to RAGatouille as a semi-official library for using ColBERT. The code is released under the MIT license.

title: Pyserini: Python toolkit for reproducible sparse and dense retrieval research
text: Pyserini is a Python toolkit for reproducible information retrieval (IR) research with sparse and dense representations. It is developed by castorini, Jimmy Lin's research group at the University of Waterloo, and is released under the Apache-2.0 license. Sparse retrieval is provided through the group's Anserini toolkit, which is built on Lucene, and covers traditional lexical models such as BM25 as well as learned sparse retrieval models such as SPLADE and uniCOIL. Dense retrieval is provided through integration with Facebook's Faiss library for vector search. Pyserini supplies prebuilt indexes so that experimental runs on standard IR test collections can be reproduced out of the box, and most features of Anserini are exposed through its Python interface. Its paper describes it as an easy-to-use toolkit that supports replicable IR research.

title: Anserini: Lucene toolkit for reproducible information retrieval research
text: Anserini is a toolkit for reproducible information retrieval (IR) research built on the Lucene search library. It is developed by castorini, Jimmy Lin's research group at the University of Waterloo, and released under the Apache-2.0 license. By building on Lucene, the project aims to close the gap between academic IR research and the practice of building real-world search applications. Anserini grew out of a 2016 reproducibility study of several open-source retrieval engines, published at ECIR, and later overview papers appeared at SIGIR and in JDIQ. The documentation explains how to reproduce experimental results both from raw document collections and from prebuilt indexes. Most of Anserini's features are also available from Python through the companion Pyserini toolkit.

title: rerankers: one Python API for cross-encoders, ColBERT, RankGPT and API rerankers
text: rerankers is a lightweight, low-dependency Python library that gives a single unified API for common reranking and cross-encoder models, whatever their architecture. It was developed by bclavie as a member of Answer.AI and is released under the Apache-2.0 license. Supported methods include any standard Sentence Transformers or Transformers cross-encoder, T5-based pointwise rankers such as MonoT5 and InRanker, RankGPT through both the original implementation and RankLLM, RankZephyr via the rank-llm library, a ColBERT-based reranker, LLM-based pointwise rankers, BAAI's BGE layerwise LLM rerankers, ONNX-optimised FlashRank models that run quickly on CPU, and MonoVLMRanker, a multimodal image reranker. It also wraps hosted reranking APIs from Cohere, Jina, Voyage, Mixedbread, Pinecone and Isaacus. The README includes an example showing how to use it inside a LangChain pipeline.

title: Sentence Transformers CrossEncoder: cross-encoder reranker models
text: The Sentence Transformers library includes a CrossEncoder class for cross-encoder models, also known as rerankers. A cross-encoder takes a pair of inputs, typically a query and a document text, and computes a similarity score for that pair; some models also accept multimodal pairs such as a text query and an image document. The documentation notes that cross-encoders generally perform better than Sentence Transformer bi-encoder models but are often slower, because they need a computation for every pair rather than for every text. For this reason they are often used to rerank the top-k results returned by a bi-encoder retriever, a retrieve-and-rerank setup. The predict method scores text pairs and the rank method orders a list of passages for a query. The usage example loads the pretrained cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 model.

title: FlashRank: lightweight CPU reranking library for search and RAG
text: FlashRank is a lightweight, fast Python library for adding a reranking step to existing search and retrieval pipelines. It needs neither PyTorch nor Transformers and runs on CPU. It supports two kinds of rerankers: pairwise or pointwise rerankers based on cross-encoders, and listwise rerankers based on LLMs. Available models include ms-marco-TinyBERT-L-2-v2 (the default), the cross-encoder ms-marco-MiniLM-L-12-v2, rank-T5-flan as a non cross-encoder option, the multilingual ms-marco-MultiBERT-L-12, ce-esci-MiniLM-L12-v2 fine-tuned on the Amazon ESCI dataset, an Arabic reranker, and a 4-bit quantised GGUF build of the rank_zephyr_7b_v1_full LLM reranker. The README describes using FlashRank after lexical search, after semantic search or RAG retrieval from vector databases, and in hybrid search. It is released under the Apache-2.0 license.

title: Elastic ELSER: learned sparse encoder for semantic search in Elasticsearch
text: ELSER, the Elastic Learned Sparse EncodeR, is a retrieval model trained by Elastic that lets you run semantic search in Elasticsearch, returning results based on contextual meaning and user intent rather than exact keyword matches. It works as a learned sparse encoder: it expands indexed passages and queries into collections of weighted terms, where the terms are learned associations capturing relevance rather than synonyms of the search words. The terms and weights are stored at index time in the Elasticsearch sparse vector (or rank features) field type. ELSER is an out-of-domain model, so it does not need fine-tuning on your own data, and it is recommended for English documents and queries. It is deployed as a trained model, ideally through the inference API, and the semantic_text workflow is the easiest way to use it. It encodes only the first 512 tokens of a field, so long texts should be chunked.

title: OpenSearch neural sparse search: sparse semantic retrieval with an inverted index
text: Neural sparse search is a semantic search method in OpenSearch that relies on sparse embedding models rather than dense text embeddings. A sparse encoding model turns text into a sparse vector, a list of token and weight pairs, and the data is ingested into a rank features index, so neural sparse search runs on an inverted index and is as efficient as BM25. OpenSearch contrasts this with dense retrieval, which uses k-NN search and consumes a lot of memory and CPU. You can configure an ingest pipeline that generates and stores sparse vector embeddings from document text at ingestion time, with query text converted for you, or you can ingest raw sparse vectors and search with them directly. A two-phase search pipeline processor can accelerate queries, and neural sparse approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search is available for sparse_vector fields using the Lucene or native engine.

title: Qdrant: SPLADE sparse vectors and hybrid search
text: This Qdrant article explains sparse vectors and SPLADE and shows how to use them in the Qdrant vector database. SPLADE is described as a class of models that learn query and document expansion, adding other relevant terms while keeping the ability to match exact words and phrases, and offering some interpretability. Qdrant supports a separate index for sparse vectors; sparse vectors need no size or distance settings, and the sparse index is kept in RAM by default. The code examples compute SPLADE vectors with Hugging Face Transformers, create a Qdrant collection with a named sparse vector, insert points and query them with query_points. Because each Qdrant point can hold both dense and sparse vectors, a single collection can serve hybrid search, where sparse vectors favor results containing the query keywords and dense vectors cover semantically similar results.

title: Ragas: open-source evaluation toolkit for RAG and LLM applications
text: Ragas is an open-source toolkit for evaluating and optimizing applications built on large language models (LLMs), including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. It is released under the Apache-2.0 license, and its citation names VibrantLabs as the author. Ragas offers both LLM-based and traditional metrics, can automatically generate test datasets covering many scenarios, integrates with LLM frameworks such as LangChain and with observability tools, and helps build feedback loops from production data. Its documented RAG metrics include context precision, context recall, context entities recall, noise sensitivity, response relevancy and faithfulness, plus multimodal faithfulness and relevance. Other metrics cover agents and tool use, such as tool call accuracy and agent goal accuracy; natural language comparison, such as factual correctness, semantic similarity, BLEU and ROUGE; SQL query evaluation; and general-purpose aspect-critic and rubric-based scoring.

title: LangChain: framework for building agents and LLM-powered applications
text: LangChain is a framework for building agents and applications powered by large language models (LLMs), published by the langchain-ai organization on GitHub under the MIT license. It connects LLMs to diverse data sources and external or internal systems through a large library of integrations with model providers, tools, vector stores, retrievers and other components. Its modular, component-based architecture is meant for quickly building and iterating on LLM applications, and it lets teams swap models in and out while experimenting. The README also highlights production features such as monitoring, evaluation and debugging. Related projects include LangGraph, a low-level agent orchestration framework; LangSmith, for agent evaluation, observability and debugging; and Deep Agents, a higher-level package built on LangChain. An equivalent JavaScript and TypeScript library, LangChain.js, is also available.

title: LlamaIndex: open-source data framework for building LLM and agentic applications
text: LlamaIndex is an open-source framework for building agentic applications, described as a data framework for building LLM apps, and is released under the MIT license. It offers data connectors that ingest existing data sources and formats such as APIs, PDFs, documents and SQL. It provides ways to structure that data into indices and graphs so it can be used easily with large language models, and an advanced retrieval and query interface over the data. Developers can customize or extend any module, including data connectors, indices, retrievers, query engines and reranking modules. A large set of integration packages works with the core library. The project also points to LlamaParse, a separate platform focused on document agents and agentic OCR, and to open benchmarking work for parsing and extraction.

title: Haystack by deepset: open-source framework for RAG, search and agents
text: Haystack, by deepset, is an open-source AI orchestration framework for building production-ready applications with large language models in Python. It is released under the Apache-2.0 license. Applications are assembled as pipelines of components; a pipeline can run synchronously or asynchronously and stream output token by token. Built-in components cover retrieval, indexing, tool calling, memory and evaluation, and developers can also write their own. Haystack targets scalable retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, multimodal applications, semantic search, question answering and autonomous agents, and agent behavior can be extended with lifecycle hooks for guardrails and custom logic. It integrates with model providers and platforms including OpenAI, Mistral, Anthropic, Cohere, Hugging Face, Google, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock and local models, among many others.

title: Faiss: library for efficient similarity search of dense vectors (Meta)
text: Faiss is a library for efficient similarity search and clustering of dense vectors, developed primarily at Meta's Fundamental AI Research group and released under the MIT license. It contains algorithms that search sets of vectors of any size, up to sets that may not fit in RAM, along with supporting code for evaluation and parameter tuning. Faiss is written in C++ with complete wrappers for Python and NumPy, and some of its most useful algorithms are implemented on the GPU, where input can come from CPU or GPU memory. Vectors are compared with L2 (Euclidean) distance or dot products. Index types range from simple baselines such as exact search, to methods based on binary vectors and compact quantization codes, to methods such as HNSW and NSG that add an indexing structure on top of the raw vectors.

title: pgvector: open-source vector similarity search for PostgreSQL
text: pgvector is an open-source PostgreSQL extension for vector similarity search that lets you store vectors together with the rest of your data, keeping Postgres features such as ACID compliance, point-in-time recovery and JOINs. By default it performs exact nearest neighbor search with perfect recall, and adding an index enables approximate nearest neighbor search, trading some recall for speed. Supported index types are HNSW, which builds a multilayer graph, and IVFFlat, which divides vectors into lists and searches a subset of them. Distance functions include L2, inner product, cosine, L1, Hamming and Jaccard distance, and it handles single-precision, half-precision, binary and sparse vectors. For hybrid search it can be combined with Postgres full-text search, with results combined using Reciprocal Rank Fusion or a cross-encoder. It can be used from any language with a Postgres client.

title: Chroma: open-source data infrastructure for AI search and retrieval
text: Chroma describes itself as open-source data infrastructure for AI, licensed under Apache 2.0. It stores documents and metadata and supports dense, sparse and hybrid search, as well as keyword and regex search over data without embeddings. Results can be filtered at query time by metadata conditions. Chroma works with many embedding models, including those from OpenAI, Cohere, Hugging Face and sentence-transformers, and can index and search images, audio and other modalities alongside text. You can run it locally, self-host it, or use Chroma Cloud, a managed serverless service, and you create a database and add data to it with the Chroma SDK. The project's GitHub README also shows a Python client installed with pip and a JavaScript client installed with npm.

title: Vespa: AI search platform for low-latency computation over large data
text: Vespa is a platform for applications that need low-latency computation over large data sets, presented as an AI search platform. It stores and indexes structured, text and vector data, and queries can search free-text fields, structured data or vector spaces with approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search, including filters combined with ANN conditions. Matches are scored by ranking expressions that can compute any business logic or machine-learned model, and the highest-scoring matches can optionally pass through a second ranking stage. Writes are persistent and visible in all queries once acknowledged, and the platform scales to more content, more expensive inference and higher query volume. Typical use cases include search, recommendation and personalization. Vespa's source code is open on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license, so it can be built and run yourself.

title: Weaviate: open-source vector database with hybrid search
text: Weaviate is an open-source, cloud-native vector database, written in Go, that stores both data objects and their vectors to enable semantic search at scale. It supports hybrid search that combines semantic vector search with traditional keyword (BM25) search, and vector search can be combined with structured filtering. Data can be vectorized at import time using integrated vectorizers from providers such as OpenAI, Cohere, Hugging Face and Google. Beyond plain retrieval, Weaviate has built-in generative search (RAG) and reranking capabilities. Vector quantization and multi-vector encoding reduce memory usage, and production deployments get built-in multi-tenancy, replication and role-based access control (RBAC) authorization. Most of the repository is available under the BSD 3-Clause License, while files in one folder require a commercial license.
